speechtext: I should like to ask a question of the Postmaster General. Have certain postal rates been increased, and some of them doubled? If so, why has parliament not been notified or consulted? How does this fit in with the economy program announced by the department?

subtopic: INCREASE OF RATES ON CIRCULARS, PRINTED MATTER, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member for Selkirk was good enough to send me notice of his question about five minutes ago.

subtopic: INCREASE OF RATES ON CIRCULARS, PRINTED MATTER, ETC.
speechtext: On a point of order, I sent it at eleven o'clock this morning.

subtopic: INCREASE OF RATES ON CIRCULARS, PRINTED MATTER, ETC.
speechtext: By post?

subtopic: INCREASE OF RATES ON CIRCULARS, PRINTED MATTER, ETC.
speechtext:
Certain postal rates have been increased recently and have been duly announced in the Canada Gazette. The rates on circulars and printed matter have been increased. The old rate was one cent for each two ounces or fraction thereof. The increased rate is two cents for the first two ounces, and one cent for each additional two ounces or fraction thereof. This old rate had been in existence since 1904. The purpose of the increase has to do with the third question the hon. member asked, because it is part of the economy program of the department. First of all it is to be used to pay off the deficit that is being encountered at the present time by the department, to the extent of about $2,250,000 on the printed matter alone. It also has to do with the economy program, in that with this increased rate it is the estimate of the department that the amount of printed matter sent by mail will be decreased by approximately twenty-five per cent, and to that extent the letter carriers will be relieved of the loads they have to carry at the present time.
The second increase that has been made is in connection with parcel post rates. This is a quite complicated matter, and has already been announced in the Canada Gazette. The third increase that has been made recently is in registration fees. They have been increased from 10 cents to 20 cents on the first $25 indemnity, and a relative increase over that amount. The average cost of registration in Canada at the present time is 23 cents. We were losing money on each one of those registrations in the lower denominations.
The hon. member's second question was as to why parliament had not been notified or consulted. According to section 7(e) of the Post Office Act, the Postmaster General has the discretion to fix the rates on all mailable matter except first-class mail, newspapers, magazines and the like. The reason, I imagine, for this discretion being given to the Postmaster General is that in connection with first-class mail, newspapers and magazines the postal department has a complete monopoly, whereas in connection with other matters, such as circulars and registration fees, parcel post and the like, we are in competition with other companies doing a similar business, and we have to have authority to act quickly if a condition develops that requires speedy action.

speakeroldname: Hon. George Prudham (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: MODIFICATION OF APPLICATION AS TO LAST QUARTER OF 1950 AND EXTENSION IN MODIFIED FORM TO 1951
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act to modify its application with reference to the last quarter of the year 1950 and to extend the application of the act in a modified form to the year 1951.
He said: Mr. Speaker, with your permission I should like to make a brief statement.
I hold that a healthy gold industry in Canada means a healthy mining industry as a whole. The search for commercial base metals and strategic minerals can most effectively and economically be carried on with the search for gold. In other words,

Gold Mining
gold mining is the stimulus which provides encouragement to search for new mineral wealth.
Much of Canada's future growth is bound up in the development and colonization of our northern country; and gold mining is the pioneer industry in opening northern Canada for development. The gold mines give employment to about 23,000 people, in addition to employees in dependent communities directly supported by them. They give further employment to large numbers in the cities and towns across Canada where mining machinery and supplies are manufactured. Our Canadian gold production provides a supply of ready foreign exchange with no marketing problem, and Canada is known among the trading nations of the world as one of the important producers of the precious metal. Gold mining is a truly Canadian venture and Canadian people control the majority of the mines.
All these facts were no doubt in the mind of the Canadian government when the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was first enacted in 1948. Its purpose was to assist the Canadian gold mine operators in restoring normal operations and in meeting the greatly increased costs of production while facing a fixed price for the industry's product. It was under these conditions that what has been termed the "cost-aid" program was commenced for a three-year period to cover the calendar years 1948, 1949 and 1950. This "cost-aid" program has definitely assisted the mines in meeting the increased costs of production and in restoring efficiency in their operations, which efficiency had been greatly impaired by the labour shortages and material restrictions of the war years.
However, throughout the years 1948, 1949 and 1950 the cost of production of gold continued to increase, and in the fall of 1950, following representations made by the gold mining industry, and after consultations with the international monetary fund, the government decided to recommend to parliament the continuance of the "cost-aid" program for another year.
The bill which it is now proposed to introduce in this house has a double purpose. The first is to provide for additional assistance covering gold produced and sold during the last quarter of 1950, to compensate for the decreased premium on the Canadian dollar. The second and most important purpose of the bill is to extend to the calendar year 1951, on a revised basis, the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.
It is expected that the "cost-aid" to be distributed to the gold mines in 1951 by

virtue of the amended act will amount to something between ten and eleven million dollars.
The hope is hereby expressed that the new program of assistance will help the gold mines to meet the continuing high costs of production, and that consequently these mines will not fail the northern communities which they.have been instrumental in setting up and which now depend wholly or largely upon the mines for survival.

subtopic: MODIFICATION OF APPLICATION AS TO LAST QUARTER OF 1950 AND EXTENSION IN MODIFIED FORM TO 1951
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I am not mistaken, this is the first bill which the minister has introduced since he attained cabinet rank. May I take advantage of this occasion to say that I am sure there is no member of the government who commands a greater measure of good will among members in all parts of the house than the minister who has just introduced the resolution.
The resolution before the house impresses us at once with its limited nature. It reads:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act to modify its application with reference to the last quarter of the year 1950 and to extend the application of the act in a modified form to the year 1951.
One cannot read those words without being impressed by the temporary nature of this measure which is re-emphasized by the resolution. The limited scope of the legislation is foreshadowed by the resolution. Apparently we are still thinking in terms of an emergency which is to be dealt with on a session-to-session basis.
I was glad to hear the minister stress the importance of the gold mining industry to innumerable communities in various parts of Canada. The minister stated that 23,000 persons are directly engaged in the gold mining industry, and I think it is fair to state that the number of persons who indirectly derive a livelihood from the operations of the gold mines is not less than 100,000.
In the days gone by also the gold mining industry has played a vital role in maintaining the economy of Canada. Those who remember the unhappy history of depression days will not have forgotten what the health of the gold mining industry in those days meant, not only to the communities adjacent to the mines, but also in providing employment in industrial areas and markets for agricultural producers in all parts of Canada.
It seems to me that there has not been in this house the recognition of the importance of this industry that it deserved. In July, 1949, Dr. Charles Camsell, the former deputy minister of mines and resources, had this to

say about the Canadian gold mining industry in a notable speech he delivered at Oxford, England. I refer to a Canadian Press dispatch of his speech reporting him as saying:
Many of Canada's legislators do not appreciate to what extent gold has been responsible for the development of Canada.
The report continues:
"The influence of gold on our Canadian economy has been vastly greater than mere production statistics would indicate," Camsell said in the paper.
A casual trip through the belt extending through northern Ontario and Quebec revealed the influence of gold deposits in developing the country and making it possible for permanent industry or agriculture to "live and thrive." Canada today needed strong mining industry more than ever before, particularly for strategic reasons. "Our production in 1948 was the greatest in our history."
I point out he is speaking of our total mineral production. He went on to conclude:
I know of nothing that will take any considerable body of population into that country-
He is speaking there of the Northwest Territories.
-except the lure of gold or some other mineral such as uranium.
Therefore I hope that in speaking on this subject this afternoon, and drawing attention to the importance of the gold mining industry and the importance to all of Canada and to people in all walks of life in Canada of the health of that industry, we shall not hear such flippant remarks as have been made sometimes in this house about serving the interests of the Toronto stock exchange and things of that kind. Let us be honest enough and realistic enough to recognize the vital importance of the gold mining industry in Canada for all Canadians.
It seems to me that the minister might have gone further and spoken of the difficulties which confront the gold mining industry today. I think it is not unfair to describe these difficulties in terms of the plight of that industry today. The minister of mines of the province of Ontario, the Hon. Welland Gemmell, said in the legislature of Ontario on February 26 of this year, as reported in the Globe and Mail of February 27:
Unless the federal government takes a realistic attitude toward gold, communities such as Kirkland Lake, Timmins, Red Lake and1 Geraldton face a serious and precarious future, mines minister Gemmell, member for Sudbury, told the legislature yesterday.
Without going into details as to what the dominion should do the minister said, "I fervently hope the near future will bring good news from the standpoint of the yellow metal."
The minister of mines of Ontario was looking forward there to an announcement from the federal government as to legislation
Gold Mining
that was to be introduced at the present session, and I am afraid that the legislation foreshadowed by the resolution now under discussion will be received with very great disappointment.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) had accurate words to describe the plight of the gold mining industry as he found it in June of 1949 during the election campaign, because in a speech at Timmins he described conditions in that gold mining community in these words: "The grim shadow of mine shutdowns that has been hanging over many gold mining properties". That was the way he described the condition. Then he went on to indicate what the present act, as it stood on the statute book in 1948, had accomplished by way of assistance to meet the situation; but he also admitted the inadequacy of the legislation because he then foreshadowed further assistance to gold, which, as hon. members will recall, was introduced in the fall of that year at the second session of 1949. Here are his further words from his speech at Timmins:
Many gold mines in Canada now are just staggering along because they are being squeezed between the fixed price of gold, $35 an ounce, and the high cost of production per ounce of gold recovered.
These words of the Prime Minister in June, 1949, can be just as accurately applied to conditions today. The fundamental problem confronting gold production in Canada today is, as indicated by the Prime Minister in that last quotation, that while costs of production have been advancing with very great rapidity and unhappy results, the price at which producers may sell their product is fixed. It is set by the government. It is not simply set by the government; it is actually tied down by the government through international agreement.
Rising costs have affected every mine, regardless of the stage of production or development. Mine development costs, mine production costs, have risen with startling effect. I am sure I do not need to say to this house that very often the narrowest kind of margin between the cost of production on the one hand and the sale price of the product on the other means the difference between turning ore into useless rock or vice versa, turning otherwise useless rock into what may be valuable ore. The position is just as simple as that.
In the extract I read the Prime Minister mentioned that the fixed price of gold at that time was $35 per ounce. You will remember, sir, that was the price fixed by the United
1G74

Gold Mining
States. That was an established United States price which found its way into international agreement when various nations entered into the Bretton Woods agreement. After devaluation of the Canadian dollar on September 20, 1949, the price in terms of the Canadian dollar was advanced by 10 per cent to $38.50, and some little benefit was enjoyed by the gold mines in consequence. But then you will remember that it was only a few months later that the government decided to set the gold mines back exactly where they had been, by reducing by an equivalent amount, namely, $3.50 per ounce, the maximum assistance allowed under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. Therefore in that respect the mines were put back in the position they had been in prior to devaluation.
I should like to say a word about the history of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, and I wish to be quite fair about it. The bill was introduced first in 1948, to assist the gold mines to overcome difficulties which at that time had become almost insuperable. The government was slow to act. The threatening situation confronting gold production in Canada had been laid before the government repeatedly in previous sessions. They moved at last in 1948. I think it is fair to say that the measure never promised to do more than render some assistance. It was never looked upon by the government as anything more than emergency legislation to contribute for a very limited period, because the period has always been limited by statute. We have literally been extending on a year-to-year basis the kind of limited assistance which the act offered.
The report of the administration of this act for the fiscal period ended March 31, 1950, had this to say in general terms in its opening paragraph:
The purpose of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was to assist Canadian gold mine operators in meeting the greatly increased costs of production of gold for which, unlike all other primary mine products, there had been no compensating increase in the price. It was designed primarily to assist the high-cost or marginal mines to continue in operation over a difficult period and also to enable such mines to continue to maintain their dependent communities.
I read that, Mr. Speaker, to emphasize that the purpose of this act was not simply to assist persons who might have had the fortune or misfortune to hold gold mining stocks. It was put forward to give some limited assistance to the industry because of the great benefits that industry brings to all
TMr. Fleming.]
Canada, and particularly to enable those gold mines to continue to maintain their dependent communities.
What has been accomplished under this act? Well, the accomplishments are limited. Assistance has been given; and to the extent of that assistance the act has been helpful. I make no attempt to deny that the legislation has been helpful as far as it has gone. With all its limitations, with all its imperfections, the act has been of assistance. For instance, in the first year of operation, 111 mines received assistance. It is perhaps significant that in the following year, 1949, the number of mines assisted dropped to 95. The report for the year ended March 31, 1951, has not yet been issued, so we do not know the total number of mines assisted in 1950. The minister did not give us that information this afternoon, but it would be interesting to learn whether that downward trend has continued or has been reversed.
In terms of amounts paid out under this act the situation is not dissimilar. In 1948 the amount of assistance provided under this act, in round figures, was $10 million. In 1949, again in round figures, it was between $12 and $13 million; and today the minister indicated that in 1950 the amount of assistance had dropped to between $10 and $11 million.
At this point I think it is fair to comment that the burden imposed on the public treasury in consequence of this act has not been very great. When you consider how readily parliament has been voting large sums of money to assist others, it seems to me that an average of $11 million over a three-year period is at most a very limited amount of assistance to an industry of such great importance to the economic welfare of all Canada.
The act has had this further drawback, that its operation has been tied to a very complicated formula. In its effect it has been quite artificial. I do not care how ingeniously the draftsmen of such legislation apply their intelligence in an endeavour to work out formulae that may be fair in their general application throughout the whole industry, I do not consider it possible for legislation of this kind to be fair to all types of mines and all types of properties under development.
In fairness to this act, let us recognize that the production of gold has increased during the period of its operation. The amount of gold produced in Canada from gold mines only, not including gold produced by base metal mines, in 1948 was 3,159,934 ounces, which represented a welcome increase over

the previous year. In 1949 gold production in Canada increased to 3,673,971 ounces from gold mines alone, and 4,123,518 including gold produced by base metal mines; and in 1950, according to a recent bulletin issued by the dominion bureau of statistics, Canada's gold production from all mines amounted to 4,448,396 fine ounces, an increase of eight per cent over the previous year. We will all welcome those increases. We will all acknowledge that this act has played some part in bringing them about. That is not to say, however, that the act is perfect or that parliament should simply stop with the enactment of amendments to it in such limited terms as are foreshadowed in the resolution now under debate.
Now may I say a word directly about this proposed amendment. We observe that it proposes simply to continue the present act for a limited period. The amendment is to modify the application of the act for the last quarter of 1950 and extend its application in a modified form to the year 1951. We have had very little indication of what the modification is to be; but again, like its predecessors in the past three sessions, this must be considered simply stop-gap, temporary legislation. Having regard to the very serious difficulties confronting the gold mining industry today; having regard, as we must have regard, to the sacrifices that are being imposed upon the gold mining industry by deliberate government policy, I think we can only regard this measure as disappointing and inadequate. Obviously it intends to continue all the present artificiality and uncertainty of government policy with respect to this important industry. We have seen changes made from year to year in the method of application, the extent of assistance or the basis of that assistance under this act. Today no gold mining operator in Canada knows what government policy in this respect is going to be at the conclusion of this calendar year. How is the gold mining industry to build for the future; how is it to expand, if it is to be confronted with all the uncertainties as to government policy and future assistance attendant upon legislation so temporary in character as that now before the house?
Again we are being asked to look at this problem as simply a temporary emergency. Apparently it is the idea of the government that the needs of the industry should be met on a hand-to-mouth basis. Where longterm policies on the part of the government and parliament are needed today, we are simply offered short-term, hand-to-mouth, stop-gap legislation.
Gold Mining
In considering the position of gold and the industry, we must have regard to recent international events. Probably the most striking development in connection with gold in the past year has been the reversal in the movement of gold with respect to the United States. There has been a reversal of the trend which had been in effect for years when the United States was, year by year, a big net importer of gold. Within the past year the United States has been transferred into an exporter of gold. That is apparently largely the result of the improvement in the economies and trade of some of the nations abroad with whom the United States has been trading. It is due in no small measure to the policy of the United States government in stockpiling materials that can only be purchased abroad.
Another fact of very great consequence amongst international events during the past year has been the firm position taken by the government of South Africa to protect the gold mining industry in that great country. You will remember, sir, that last May the government of South Africa announced it was no longer going to be bound to sell its gold at the price fixed by the international monetary fund, the agency established for this purpose under the Bretton Woods agreement. The statement made in the parliament of South Africa by the minister of finance, Mr. Havenga, is reported by the Associated Press, in a dispatch from Capetown dated May 5, 1950, as follows:
South Africa has reserved the right to sell its gold at the highest price it can get in the world's free markets contrary to the wishes of the international monetary fund.
N. C. Havenga, finance minister in a strong statement to parliament tonight, expressed the nationalist government's dissatisfaction with the board of directors of the fund. Wednesday the board rejected a South African proposal that gold producers be permitted to sell half their output in free markets at the best price obtainable above the fixed monetary price of $35 an ounce.

Sir, I think in addition that we underestimated at that time the place, the high importance, the almost necessary position, of gold in facilitating the trade of the world; and we certainly had no expectation at that time that trading conditions would be bedevilled and defeated by the erection of this iron curtain, by aggression and machinations on the part of the tyrants in the Kremlin.
I wish to make one or two further brief observations, sir, about the way in which this agreement has worked out. It is not unfair, I think, to say that the policy of the international monetary fund has been largely dominated by the United States. It has been influenced to a considerable extent also by policy of the government of the United Kingdom. I do not believe any one of us can think that Canadian interests have played a very important part in the shaping of policy on the part of the international monetary fund. Canada is a producer. Its net position is overwhelmingly on the production side. The United States' net position has been, with the exception of the past year, that of an importer. Great Britain has been historically an importer of gold.
Now, how can you reconcile the fundamental divergence of interests of these nations under a scheme such as this? I think one result has been, sir, to shackle a very important arm of Canadian production. Another has been pressure on certain forms of the Canadian economy, and the introduction of further measures of artificiality in a situation that we had already made artificial by national and international policy in 1945.
I believe the time has come, sir, when parliament must re-examine the whole position of gold and the price of gold. I believe
Gold Mining
Canada must ask herself, and we in this House of Commons must ask ourselves: are we interested in obtaining a better price for our product?-because we are not obtaining for it today the value of it. We are selling it below the price that it would bring us if those shackles imposed by national and international policy were struck off.
In reviewing and re-examining Canada's interest in this issue, please do not misunderstand me; I am not taking a narrow view in measuring where our interest lies. I am not saying that simply because the price of gold in the free market of the world is considerably higher than the fixed price at which we are compelled to sell to the Royal Canadian Mint or for export, that alone must determine all the details of Canadian national policy. But I think we must give due weight to those facts.
Now, there are two further factors, which are deserving of consideration. I am always conscious of the fact, sir, as I am sure all members of this house are, that in any aspect of our economic life where we are brought into close contact with the United States, we must not take a narrow view of the particular issue. We must weigh it against the benefit of those broad measures of co-operation between this country and the United States which are not only the hope of this continent, but to a very large extent underwrite the hopes of the whole world; therefore, sir, I am not proposing that we proceed in any aggressive or shortsighted manner in this respect. But I do wish to be sure that Canadian interests in a matter of this kind, closely related as we are to the United States, and suffering as we are today by reason of the supremacy of the United States' interest in the administration of the international monetary fund-I want to be sure that sacrifices are not being imposed unfairly on some particular branch of Canadian production. It seems to me the case is unanswerable that unfair sacrifices are being imposed upon the Canadian gold mining industry; and when we are importing inflation from the United States, I wonder whether it would not be justifiable on our part to try to better our position by getting a better price for this important product of ours when it is sold to the big and friendly importer to the south of us.
Why should the Canadian gold mining industry be made to pay the price-and a heavy price it is-for national and international policy, particularly when, as it seems to me, sir, we must open our eyes and see that these policies are defeating their rightful purpose and must be re-examined and revised?

Gold Mining
The other question is this. We must take into account in all fairness the possibility of inflation in Canada in consequence of an increase in the price of gold. Now, sir, there are many who associate the idea of an increase in the general price level with an increase in the price of gold. That idea probably dates back to the early 1930's, when President Roosevelt increased the price of gold as a means of trying to counteract the strong deflationary influences at work at that time in the United States. But, sir, who can stand in this house today and contend that to permit the Canadian gold production to earn more money for Canada is going to have an inflationary effect on the Canadian economy? I say, sir, that there is no one who can argue that proposition with any confidence. I do not believe there is proof available to anyone that an increase today in the price of Canadian gold would have an inflationary effect on the level of general commodity prices in Canada. On the other hand, I can think of a great deal of benefit that would result from an increase in the price of gold we export, and the way in which the consequent results can be applied to counteract the importation of inflation into this country from the United States.
Sir, I think the direction in which we must move in Canada today is toward greater freedom in trying to enable gold to yield its fair value in the markets of the world. Bear in mind that I am not for one minute saying -and I am trying to make this abundantly clear-that we should just cut loose from the international monetary fund, or that we should ignore our commitments there, or that we should proceed without due regard to the broad question of our relations with the United States or to other aspects of the effect of such measures on our economy. But, sir, I say that the case, on balance, is overwhelming for a substantial movement at the present time in the direction of a freer market for Canadian gold. And as long as we are going to have agreements such as the international monetary fund shackling an important wing of the Canadian economy it seems to me that the duty of this parliament is clear, namely, to face courageously and honestly the limitations, the drawbacks, the weaknesses, the handicaps of the international monetary fund, and address ourselves to seeking a correction and amendment of them.
I do not think for one moment that we can any longer submit to a mere continuation of the present structure and policy of the international monetary fund. Unless there is some change in the price of gold at which we may sell our production in the markets of the world, then it seems to me that we must

pound on the doors of the international monetary fund, and of those responsible for its administration. And unless there is some change in their policy, then I think this parliament must be prepared to take action.
I hope the house will not fail to recognize the importance of gold both in our economy and as the means of exchange throughout the world. Gold is still what it has been for a long time, the universally accepted medium of international exchange. It is still sought by all the nations of the world today, and not least of all by Russia herself. There have been times in recent years when the United States dollar undertook to challenge gold as the accepted medium of international exchange. Sir, I think that time is past, when we see today the way in which inflation has weakened the value of the United States dollar, and the way in which gold has been moving in the net position away from the United States.
Let me say further that I think it is high time the foreign exchange control board re-examined its holdings in its reserves. I think it is high time that due regard should be had by the board for the fact that the United States dollar has not the value it had before, either in terms of its intrinsic purchasing power or in terms of the prestige and confidence attached to it in the world. I think the time has come when the reserves of the foreign exchange control board, to a degree far greater than has been the fact hitherto, should take the form of gold and not United States dollars. I think the time has come when, on the part of those administering the foreign exchange control board in this country, there has to be a recognition of the importance of building up those reserves in the form of gold rather than in United States dollars.
If we are going to cling to any hope of re-establishing the kind of world to which we looked forward in 1945, we must have regard to the place of gold as a means of assisting the convertibility of currencies, with all the attendant benefits that has for the trade of the world, and in particular for a country like Canada which has trading relations with the two great trading blocs in the world, the sterling bloc and the dollar bloc.
Lastly, I hope the government will not deny to the house the opportunity of reviewing the whole of our national policy with respect to gold. Those who sat in the committee on banking and commerce in the fall of 1945 will never forget the importance of those hearings, and the way in which

members of parliament informed themselves, with, of course, considerable assistance from Mr. Louis Rasminsky, a very distinguished Canadian economist, whom we all respect. That was five and a half years ago: conditions have changed vastly since that time. I hope an opportunity will be afforded, through the medium of a committee like our committee on banking and commerce, to review the matter in detail, and with all the evidence that is required or relevant before us, so that we may review and re-examine the whole question of international and national policy with respect to gold.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has rendered a distinct service to the people of Canada and the House of Commons in his remarks this afternoon. So far as I know this is the first time since 1945, when the Canadian parliament in a fit of complete hysteria allowed itself to be precipitated into the Bretton Woods agreement, that any member of parliament, other than Social Credit "cranks", has undertaken to call in question the validity of the Bretton Woods agreement. The hon. member has not meant to call in question the validity of that agreement; he has simply undertaken to show the house and country how the agreement just cannot possibly work to the advantage of Canada, or any other nation in the world except the United States.
I should like to draw to the attention of the house and the people of Canada the absolutely preposterous position in which the Canadian parliament now finds itself. First I would read the innocent little resolution we are now debating:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act to modify its application with reference to the last quarter of the year 1950 and to extend the application of the act in a modified form to the year 1951.
I would say in a general way that if parliament does not have complete authority to pass that resolution, then it has abdicated its power to be a sovereign parliament of a sovereign nation like Canada. That must be obvious, without further argument.
Yet the minister, when introducing the resolution, used these words, if my memory serves me correctly, "that after consultation with the international monetary fund the government decided to recommend to parliament a continuance of the cost-debt program for another year."
I take it that this means that the government would hardly dare introduce this measure without the consent of the international monetary fund. Hon. members may reflect
Gold Mining
upon these facts themselves. Take those facts in the light of the observations so ably expressed this afternoon by the hon. member for Eglinton, and then meditate upon the condition of affairs in which we find ourselves. I do not propose to speak in any extended fashion in the matter this afternoon. I shall merely make this observation, based upon the remarks of the hon. member for Eglinton and of the minister, that each of these hon. gentlemen has undertaken to say that the welfare of the whole mining industry of Canada is in large measure involved with the welfare of the gold mining industry.
What does that mean? It means that without the consent of the international monetary fund this country is unable to take measures designed to benefit the mining industry, which is one of the major industries of the nation.
May I say a word or two with reference to the question I asked the hon. member for Eglinton. Perhaps it was a mean question to ask a man who was speaking on the subject to which the hon. member was then directing his remarks. But I felt it was a question that ought to be asked of a gentleman as learned as the hon. member for Eglinton, and as able as he has shown himself to be during the years of his sojourn in parliament.
One of the assumptions the house adopted was that the international monetary fund and the bank for international settlements would somehow aid in the convertibility of currency in the world. To a person adequately informed regarding the fundamental principles of international trade and the international convertibility of currency; and likewise moderately informed concerning the restrictions and regulations in the Bretton Woods agreement, the assumption that that agreement could in any way, even in the remotest degree, aid in the international convertibility of currency, is utterly preposterous.
Members of this group laid down the fundamental principles time and again in December of 1945. I challenged any man in the Dominion of Canada, inside this house or out, to point to a single flaw in the fundamental reasoning of the Social Credit group on that occasion. Every principle was absolutely sound and in accordance with the best information concerning international trade and international convertibility of currencies. In effect we laid down this principle-I am going to illustrate it by citing an experience this country has had-that it is utterly impossible to make British pounds convertible into United States dollars unless the United States are prepared to accept a sufficient amount of British goods to render the moneys of the two countries equivalent in value. It is the

acceptance of goods and the selling of goods that governs the value of world currencies.
As this group indicated, and as hon. members fully know, the United States is the most powerful factor in world economy today, largely because of her tremendous population, her tremendous productive potential and the near approach she is capable of to selfsufficiency. When a nation is self-sufficient or nearly so it does not need to take in foreign goods. All it needs to be concerned with is selling its own goods. We laid down the principle time and time again that the primary concern of the United States administration in seeking to obtain general acceptance of Bretton Woods was to enable the United States to sell her goods in the world markets. That fact remains incontrovertible today.
Will anyone tell us how in the world the acceptance of Bretton Woods can contribute in the slightest degree to the convertibility of British pounds into United States dollars? Where is the stipulation in Bretton Woods which would so operate? The world has been afflicted by what I would almost call a tragic shortage of United States dollars ever since the Bretton Woods agreement was accepted, and that alone is incontrovertible evidence of the truth of what I am saying.
I should like to say a brief word regarding inflation. Yesterday the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in that jaunty way of his made a remark to the effect that this inflation was a world phenomenon. Of course it is a world phenomenon. I believe I shall ask the Minister of Finance before we finish this session to show why there is a world phenomenon of inflation and to show to what extent the Bretton Woods agreement has contributed to that world phenomenon. In fact I may ask him to show where we should be wrong in assuming that the Bretton Woods agreement is a major factor in the production of worldwide inflation.
Before I close I should like to make this general comment on the remarks of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). He was not in the chamber when I paid him a compliment a minute or two ago.

The United States absolutely will not accept any more goods than she needs. Any goods that come into that country and which compete with goods produced by the people of the United States will be shut out ultimately. When she is in position to almost completely support herself, except in time of war, what conceivable reason can there be for believing that she will accept enough goods to render English pounds convertible into United States dollars?
Turning now to the Bretton Woods agreement: Can the Bretton Woods agreement, or a carload of such agreements, contribute even in the slightest degree to causing the United States to accept more British goods, or more Canadian goods, or more French goods, or more goods of any other nation? To ask the question of intelligent members, such as those now sitting before me, is to have them answer it with a thunderous "no". The measure of the efficacy of Bretton Woods in contributing to the convertibility of currencies is just completely zero. It can cause trouble to nations, as the hon. member for Eglinton has shown, in connection with the production in Canada of gold; it can interfere with trade, as it already has done, and render the situation infinitely more complex for such struggling nations as Great Britain and France and Germany; it can bring about an inflation that nobody knows what to do with. But it cannot possibly contribute in the slightest degree to the well-being of the nations of the world. That statement goes on Hansard with an open invitation to anyone who thinks he can answer it to do so. I will be right here through the remainder of the debate and right to the end of the session, if it is the Lord's will.
