That is all I think that I would care to say at the moment. As I said at the beginning, the discussions at this stage have usually been of a general nature, and we welcome discussions of that kind at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I am
glad to have that statement from the minister because in these estimates for the year the reduction of $28,500,000 did seem a very heavy decrease. I had anticipated it would not be that much after the supplementary estimates had been tabled that the minister speaks of. But there is a matter that I should

like to make reference to at this time because on another occasion many statements were made that agriculture, especially in western Canada, has had a period of five of the most prosperous years in the history of this country.
However, that discussion referred only to income. I never heard the Minister of Agriculture or any other minister say that these farmers had also gone through a period of five of the most expensive production years in the history of this country. I think that should be brought out.
The reason that I want to deal with this now in particular is that we had one of the minister's colleagues, the Minister of Justice, addressing several farm meetings throughout the province of Manitoba, in fact in Marquette, his own constituency. I thought probably he was briefed by the Minister of Agriculture. If not, certainly he had followed him very attentively on some occasions because his arguments were very difficult to follow through by anyone who was a farmer, at least.
He pointed out how well off the farmers had been through those five years and are today, the most prosperous period in the history of this country. But he never referred to the greatly increased production costs of those five years, and to the increase in cost right today.
I know the minister believes in the small family farm. I think most of us do. But those statements about this prosperous period are not true for the small family farm in this country. The large opertaor with modern equipment may be getting along, and may be having a prosperous time of it, but I hold in may hand the Economic Annalist, put out by the Department of Agriculture, dated December, 1950. At page 137 we find the following heading:
The Farm Business in the Gilbert Plains and Sifton Areas of Manitoba. 1949
It is a survey by J. G. MacKenzie and T. O. Riecken, and reads as follows:
The investigation of the farm business in the Gilbert Plains and Sifton areas is part of a comprehensive inquiry into economic and social problems associated with the utilization of land in Manitoba.
Farther on in the page it states:
The business year 1948-49. The period covered by the farm business record was June 1, 1948, to May 31, 1949. The 1948 crop year was a normal one for this area in which crop yields are fairly stable.
Then on page 138, dealing with the farm size and tenure it says:
The farms of the area are small; nearly half are farms of one-quarter section, slightly more than a third are half-section farms and the remainder are

larger than a half-section. The average size was 300 acres in the Gilbert Plains area and 257 in the Sifton area.
These areas are in the federal constituency of Dauphin, bordering on Marquette, the riding represented by the Minister of Justice, who was making these speeches. It is right alongside that area. There are several pages of this, giving very useful detail.
Then on page 139 there is a table showing the average farm capital in the Gilbert Plains and Sifton areas for the years 1948 and 1949. It shows real estate, machinery and equipment, livestock, feeds and1 supplies and seed. In the Gilbert Plains area the average per farm was $15,837; the average in the Sifton area was $8,341.
Then it deals with the average livestock of various kinds per farm, and on page 140 it says:
The cost of operating and repairing all farm machinery and equipment averaged $498 in the Sifton area and $1,018 in the Gilbert Plains area. If the costs of depreciation and investment in machinery were added to the current operating costs, these figures would probably be increased about 40 per cent.
Then page 141 deals with the size of the farms and the labour income. Table 5 follows which shows that in the Gilbert Plains area this survey was conducted on 81 farms and in the Sifton area on 80 farms, which was a fair number for a detailed survey. On page 142 we find the following:
While the farms of the Gilbert Plains area are generally more productive than the farms of the Sifton area, the returns from the quarter-section farms in both areas are generally too low to provide sufficient surplus to provide for the living of the operator and his family. After allowing for an average expenditure for living expenses of $939 in the Gilbert Plains area and $916 in the Sifton area, the net income on these farms in the former area was minus $208, and in the latter area minus $240, which indicates that part of the cost of maintaining the family could not be paid out of current farm revenue. The half-section farms at Sifton had a net income of $160 and at Gilbert Plains the same size farm had a net income of $469 over living Expenses.
That is a survey carried out by officials of the department itself, and I think it should be proof of how prosperous many of these farmers have been throughout those years, and are today.
May I say a word as to present conditions? We have had considerable alarm throughout the country with respect to the rapidly rising increase in the cost of living. It increased steadily month by month for the twelve months of 1950. It has been increasing much more rapidly since the first of this year. We had an increase announced just the other day, bringing the index up to 179-7-a terrific increase there. That is
Supply-Agriculture
very burdensome on all the people of this nation. The statistical survey of the Bank of Canada for February, 1950, gives the farm prices of agricultural products. It is a very interesting chart, because while it shows the average through Canada for 1950 of 249-3, it gives the averages by provinces. If you take these figures and compare them with the final month of the year it will give you a picture of the trend throughout the various parts of this nation. I will give the provinces. For 1950 the average in Prince Edward Island was 188-3; for Nova Scotia, 206-2; for New Brunswick, 216; for Quebec, 260-6; for Ontario, 264-7; for Manitoba, 255-5; for Saskatchewan, 226-4; for Alberta, 253-9; for British Columbia, 243-8; and then the average that I spoke of for all Canada, 249-3.
Then for December of 1950, that month alone the provinces showed up as follows: Prince Edward Island, 181-6; Nova Scotia, 213-6; New Brunswick, 217-9; Quebec, 276-5; Ontario, 276-8; Manitoba, 238-6; Saskatchewan, 199-7; Alberta, 237-3; British Columbia, 259-3. The average for Canada for that month was 245-4. Now, then, in relationship the fact that the national income for agriculture decreased about 12 points last year is rather significant. In round figures it means that in the last month of 1950 the agricultural income of the province of Quebec increased 16 points while in the same month in Manitoba there was a decrease of 17 points, and in Saskatchewan a decrease of 26 points. So that it shows the trend throughout the nation. These are both government journals from which I have been quoting. One of them is produced by the Department of Agriculture-I am referring to the Economic Annalist-and the other by the Bank of Canada. I do not think anyone disputes those figures.
These figures are proof that agriculture is slipping in these last few years in the matter of income. The survey made in central Manitoba is proof that the small family farm operator is still up against a pretty	tough proposition.	All the
statements which have been made in the house and on the hustings during the Easter recess are not borne out by the facts as set forth either by the Department of Agriculture itself or by the Bank of Canada. I thought this was the time and place to give those figures and to make the necessary correction, because when I was home at Easter I heard such a great amount of agitation among the people and, I will admit, a great deal of confused thinking and discussion. That is not to be wondered at. As I travelled on the trains and busses, and on the street ears in

Supply-Agriculture
Winnipeg I found that people, whether they were farmers or not, were talking about a previous debate on a very important matter connected with agriculture that had taken place just before the Easter recess. Those people said they were entitled to be confused in their discussion, and they did not think it would be any worse than the discussion that took place in the house between the ministers and members of parliament for a couple of weeks before the Easter recess.
I want to tell the committee that, at least in the prairie provinces, there is great concern about the plight of the agriculturist, on the average. I am not denying the fact that some agricultural operators with modern equipment are getting by pretty well. But the great majority of the farmers, those on the small holdings, as is borne out by this booklet from the Department of Agriculture, are having a very tough time of it. Many of them are not able to provide a living for their families from their farms.
I wish to put those facts on the record. I know we will wait expectantly for a statement from the minister before these estimates are passed as to what agriculture may expect in the near future, in these most harrowing times with which many farmers are having to contend right now. I wished also to put this information on the record because there are many people who blame the high cost of living on the farmer and, in the majority of cases, that is not the situation. I wish to make it clear, if possible, that the farmer is not to blame in many instances for the greatly increased cost of living.
At another time I referred to an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune dealing with prices in Minneapolis and Winnipeg. I did not go into detail because I thought it would be out of order. I have not the chart before me now. However, one hon. member from Saskatchewan found fault with me for criticizing what the farmers were receiving in Winnipeg. The point borne out by the article was that there is something wrong in this country in connection with processing and cost to the consumer, as compared with what farm producers get.
For most of the commodities referred to in the article appearing in the Tribune the farm producer in the United States near Minneapolis was receiving more for his raw products than was the farmer in western Canada. Yet when the farm or urban wife over there went to purchase a processed article she was able to do so at a cheaper price in Minneapolis than it could be purchased in Winnipeg.
That is the point I am trying to make. I have repeated it in two or three years and given statistics to prove it-that there is

something radically wrong in so far as the middleman in this country is concerned. While over there the farmer is much better paid for his raw materials; his wife-and the same applies to the urban wife-can purchase many of those articles for less than they can be bought in this country. That is a condition which should be rectified to some extent.
I hope that after some discussion the minister will give us some lead as to what agriculture may expect in the future. Let me say that agriculture can be depended upon to produce for this nation and to have a surplus of many goods for the underfed nations of other countries. It is most important at a time like this, when the production of essentials is so greatly needed.

Mr. Chairman, I was sorry to see a reduction in the estimates for the Department of Agriculture. Even after the minister's explanation I was sorry to note a reduction of $12 million in the estimates for agriculture during the current year. I know that in view of our defence program every possible saving will have to be made in the various departments but I do think that a healthful agricultural industry, geared to full production, should and must be an important part of our defence program.
I do not think it is a service to agriculture to be cutting the estimates of the minister's department by about 15 per cent. I agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Souris, that agriculture at this time faces many grave problems. While the prices for many agricultural products are high, nevertheless agricultural costs are increasing by leaps and bounds. Looking at our prospective markets for the future and our available markets today it does not seem at all certain that agricultural markets are in any sense guaranteed.
I am sorry that as a nation we have not been able to hold the British market for bacon or apples, or other important farm commodities. It is true that, so far, we are getting by through utilizing the Canadian and the American markets to a greater extent. But it does seem to me that the British market, which has been our best outlet in the past, is of great importance for the future, and every effort should be made to regain our position there.
One point I would emphasize, and which I feel is a real threat to Canadian agriculture both in the east and on the prairies, is the great difficulty western farmers are now having in marketing their grain. The eastern producer is interested in getting western oats, barley and wheat. The government is paying a considerable amount of money by way of freight assistance. But before this grain

can be of value to agriculture in eastern Canada it has to be moved from the prairie provinces to the lakehead, and by boats to ports in Ontario and other markets in the world. At this time we are faced with the most severe box car shortage in our history; and unless something is done, and done soon, to solve the box car problem on the prairies, we are going to find millions and millions of bushels of grain rotting in the bins, because much of that grain is damp or tough.
It was promised by the Minister of Transport that this serious agricultural problem would be dealt with. The minister assured us that the railways were co-operating and that no stone would be left unturned to improve the situation, even if our Canadian box cars had to be sent back empty from the United States. That statement was made on February 19, and just three days before statistics were published indicating that
29.000	Canadian box cars were in the United States. Approximately a month after that statement was made, on March 15, the date of the last available statistics, there were
4.000	more Canadian box cars in the United States, or a total of 33,000. The net position of the excess of Canadian box cars in the United States increased within that one month period by 2,400 even when we were told that this serious situation was going to be corrected and dealt with.
The Saskatchewan wheat pool estimate that in order to move grain from the prairies to eastern Canada between now and the end of the crop year 1,200 box cars will be required daily. Last year there were only 600 box cars used daily, but this year it looks as though we are not going to have even 600 cars daily unless something is done about this serious situation. We need twice as many box cars as we had last year and we have not nearly as many cars as we had a year ago.
The Saskatchewan wheat pool has called upon the government to appoint a controller to handle the box car situation and to see that our Canadian box cars are returned from the United States, I remember a few years ago when the problem was the other way around and we were retaining United States box cars. If my memory serves me correctly a Mr. Eric Johnston was appointed controller and he placed an embargo on United States cars coming to Canada. The result was that United States cars in Canada were soon sent home. I think it is time the government appointed a controller and put an embargo on Canadian box cars going to the United States in order to bring about a return of Canadian box cars from that country.
Supply-Agriculture
The Minister of Agriculture is a man of considerable ability in a great many ways and I am sure that he would have some influence on the government in seeing that something was done about this matter. I am taking advantage of this first opportunity since the announcement made by the Saskatchewan wheat pool to ask the minister to use his influence with his colleagues in the cabinet in order to have this shortage of box cars corrected, and to ensure that we have sufficient box cars between now and July 31, the end of the crop year, to move all the grain off the farms to the head of the lakes, to the eastern feeders and to the export markets of the world so that this food, which is such a valuable commodity at this time, will not be allowed to spoil on our western farms.
I would hope that the Minister of Agriculture could give the committee some idea as to what the government is doing to remedy this situation. Another statement by the Minister of Transport, if it does no more good than his statement on February 19, will only result in a greater number of Canadian box
cars going to the United States. That minister told us that the problem was going to be dealt with, that not a stone would be left unturned to see that we had sufficient box cars to handle the shipment of Canadian grain. Nothing has resulted from that statement except that the situation is much worse. Therefore I ask the Minister of Agriculture to tell us what the government is likely to do in order that grain on western farms may be brought to market and not be in danger of spoiling this spring.

speechtext: The point of ord-er is well taken. The question has already been decided by the house, and- there is nothing in the estimates concerning this matter.

There is plenty to talk about without going further, but I will just -say that the result of the whole set-up has

been that the wheat growers paid directly as a subsidy to the consumers of Canada 30 cents a bushel on every bushel of wheat that the Canadian consumers used throughout that period. There have been criticisms from eastern Canada and other parts. Therefore I urge every single member of the house to take into consideration that that fact actually occurred. We will leave that aspect of it. When you take 30 cents a bushel-and I am passing rapidly to bow to your decision-on 160 million bushels you have $48 million, and that is what all the farmers of western Canada believe ought to be given as the bare minimum remuneration for that most astonishing procedure.
There are five main considerations which I believe ought to be borne in mind in- dealing with the problem of the farmers of western Canada. In the first place-and this again touches on the first point but it will be the last one that will touch on the question of the $48 million-the $65 million was only part -payment of the amount of money which was absolutely -stolen by the government from Canadian farmers raising wheat, and "stolen" is the word. No communist ever did any worse than to seize vast hundreds of millions of dollars from producers, and there is no question, that it was done. The matter can be established; and will be established just as- soon as- this question is in such order that the Minister of Agriculture cannot object.
Western wheat growers have paid huge sums in taxes. When we were discussing the $65 -million item not very long ago you would have thought that every single dollar to pay that amount was coming out of Ontario.
A lot of it did, just about half.
Of course it did but you must understand that a lot of it came out of the west. In a few minutes I am going to give some facts which are just as strong as the ones the hon. member for Souris gave.
How about Temiscouata?

We will come to Temiscouata in due time. I tell you, Mr. -Chairman, that what has happened out there is a matter that simply must be recognized. If we have got to stay here until next December to get everybody in the -house to understand this matter we will stay here until we do, because we westerners simply cannot be kicked around the way we are being kicked around by people who do not understand our problem.
The next point developed by the hon. member for Souris was well taken. The farmers are not well off notwithstanding the propaganda that has been spread abroad

throughout the country. The farmers once again, Mr. Chairman-and I presume this is completely in order-are being forced right now to subsidize the people of Canada, Great Britain and thirty-seven other countries right now to the extent of 37 cents a bushel on every bushel of wheat consumed in those countries.
The Canadian farmer is much worse off than the farmer in the United States, as the hon. member for Souris pointed out. I propose to give some facts to bear out the statements I have made which hon. members can read at their convenience. Perhaps I shall be out of order if I read the first one, Mr. Chairman. It is a statement by the Alberta wheat pool on March 16, 1951, bearing upon the question of the necessity of the $48 million being paid. If that is out of order I simply will not read it now but I will do so at a later time.
Let me come to the matter of taxation. I want to say that since I have been in this house I have never objected to any favour given to any part of the Dominion of Canada. I have always supported hon. members in their contentions. Dear me, if they are suffering losses in the production of their apples I would be the first one to support something to help them, and the same with fishing or any other product of the Dominion of Canada.
If the producers of the goods that make Canada what she is are suffering, and therefore unable to produce those goods, that fact is one of the most serious considerations for the whole of the Dominion of Canada whose wealth and well-being are directly related to the production of goods by every group of producers throughout the nation. When I speak directly to some members from other parts of the country-and I hope I do not have to-I trust they will remember that I have been here fifteen years and I have seen the Canadian parliament in operation for all of those fifteen years.
Too long.

I realize it is too long for some hon. members. They would give a lot if they could get me out of here but my constituents have not felt that way. Here is an article written by Chester A. Bloom, and I imagine easterners will accept this man because he seems to be a quite popular and respected writer. The article is to be found in the Lethbridge Herald for March 24, and must have appeared in a great many other papers. The heading is "The Prairie Farmers Pay". The article reads:
During the five-year wheat pool including the four-year Canada-U.K. wheat agreement, while selling their wheat to Britain at cut-rate prices, the prairie farmers paid 77 per cent of all the farm
Supply-Agriculture
income taxes in Canada. During the four years of the U.K. wheat agreement, 1946-49 inclusive, the prairie farmers paid 81 per cent of all the farm income taxes paid in Canada.
These are the very men to whom you are giving $65 million now.
May I ask a question? Who hires Chester A. Bloom?
You may ask all the questions you desire.
Who hires Chester A. Bloom?
You may ask all the questions you desire.
That is a straight question. Who hires Chester A. Bloom?

How in the name of common sense do you imagine I know, or anybody else? The hon. member's question if it is anything at all is a direct insult to Chester A. Bloom. It presupposes that Chester A. Bloom will not tell the truth. The hon. member had better be careful to get his facts right before he challenges the figures that are given here. Meanwhile, may I tell the hon. member that is one of the cheapest questions I have ever been asked on the floor of the house, and especially coming from a man from the prairies.
On a point of order, it is not a cheap question.
It is.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, it is in order for hon. members to raise points of order in this house. The hon. member is just making a speech for his constituents and I am getting rather tired of it.
You will get a lot more tired. Let us hear the point of order.
The point of order is that you cannot cast a reflection upon an hon. member.

The hon. member cast the reflection upon himself; I cannot do any better than he did. As I said a moment ago, the amount paid in those four years by the western wheat growers was $48,254,000 out of a total of $59,489,000 paid in farm income taxes from coast to coast in Canada. I continue quoting from Chester Bloom's article:
The farmers of the three prairie provinces were getting gypped two ways-their wheat was sold at bargain prices while they carried more than three-quarters of the farm tax load in Canada.
The answer is easy-their wheat was sold by a government board. The government tax collectors knew every cent of their income-not so with all

Supply-Agriculture
the other farmers of Canada. No wonder governments like handling farm products through boards.
The 1950 farm tax returns are not yet available. But the prairie farmers have been paying an average of more than $12 million a year in farm income taxes. Their 1950 taxes will surely be up to the average so, during the five-year pool into which the government is making a $65 million final payment, the prairie farmers will have paid taxes in that period within $5 million of the $65 million.
It is quite obvious why the government did not use these figures to rebut some of the $65 million criticisms. It is one of the big national tax scandals of Canada.
Remember, this is an easterner talking, and he is talking so all easterners may hear him.
Here are some of the figures culled from a return furnished February 22 last by the Department of National Revenue answering a question asked in the house by H. R. Argue, M.P., Assiniboia:
In 1946, the total farm income taxes collected in Canada were $9,843,000 of which prairie farmers, largely wheat growers, paid $8,143,000 or 82-5 per cent.
1947-	Total Canadian farm income taxes collected, $13,581,000; prairie farmers paid $10,567,000 or 77 per cent.
1948-	Total Canadian farm income taxes collected, $18,095,000; three prairie provinces paid farm income taxes of $14,168,000 or 78 per cent.
We didn't make any money in the east.

Well, remember that this is not a sign that they were making money. After they paid their income taxes and looked after all the other details most of these people had no money left.
1949-	Total Canadian farm income taxes collected $17,970,000; three prairie provinces farm taxes, $15,385,000 or 85 per cent.
The only provinces which came anywhere near approaching these prairie records of farm income taxes were the immensely wealthy farming province of Ontario whose farmers in 1949 paid $1,940,000 in farm income taxes while British Columbia farmers paid $544,000. Quebec farmers paid only $51,000. The smaller populated maritime provinces that year paid farm income taxes of; Prince Edward Island $4,000; Nova Scotia, $33,000; New Brunswick, $11,000; and Newfoundland, $2,000.
Even before the Canadian wheat board had records of prairie farmers' wheat receipts, however, the three prairie provinces were furnishing since 1941 more than 50 per cent of the total farm income taxes collected in Canada. Here are the records 1941 to 1945 inclusive:
1941-Total farm income taxes collected, $1,592,000; prairie payments, $860,000; 1942-total farm income taxes paid, $3,372,000; prairie payments, $2,045,000; 1943-total for Canada, $11,630,000; prairies paid $8,563,000; 1944-total for Canada, $20,482,000; prairies paid, $16,838,000; 1945-total for Canada, $13,392,000; prairies paid $8,047,000.
I guess the hon. member who wanted to ask me a question feels a little unnecessary now. I do not need any authority attached to those figures; they stand on their own feet.
There are other difficulties still, in addition to the points made by the hon. member for

Souris. As I was saying, there exists a general idea that the western farmers are well off. The statement by the hon, member for Souris indicated that general impression. I would commend the admirable work of the Minister of Justice in giving those very speeches to which objection was taken, because he faced the whole situation honestly and straightforwardly and showed that Britain was not in any way responsible for the difficulties in which the prairie farmers find, themselves. That is a great thing, because if we can find out just who is responsible we shall know upon whom to call to discharge the responsibility.
Now I should like to point out just how well off the farmers were with this $1.83 a bushel. The Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out-and this is not intended as any reflection on him-that $1.83 was probably the very best payment the farmers had received; and I think the Minister of Justice pointed this out also. Let us see. I am quoting from the Searle Grain Company letter-
Oh, oh.

I hear a lot of silly
cackling, but the Searle Grain Company can give accurate figures as well as anyone else. They interpret the figures in their own way and I have no sympathy with the way that company interprets the figures.

I am going to
raise another point of order. You cannot read the Searle grain report in this house, because it changes every week, as every farmer knows. I am getting tired of these constant reports. If you agree with the Searle Grain Company, say so.

The hon. member must
be quite ill tonight; he does not seem able to get things straight in his mind. I think he will be quite surprised when he reads his remarks in Hansard tomorrow.
I am raising the point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member is quite
in order.

I am reading now from
the Searle Grain Company letter of March 28, 1951, on page 2:
Some people are saying that prairie wheat growers must be quite well off because they have received for five years an average price for their wheat of $1.83, which is a higher price, it is alleged, than has been registered in the history of grain marketing for any five years.
These speakers forget one important fact, that farmers do not live on price, but only on what price

will buy, and that the Canadian dollar has suffered a serious depreciation in purchasing power in recent years, to the extent, according to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics publication entitled "Price Index Numbers of Commodities and Services Used by Farmers, Basis 1935-39," that $1.83 is worth today no more than approximately 86 cents, and that $1.83 has had on the five years average a purchasing power of only $1.03 in terms of the purchasing power in 1935-39. The 61 years of recorded official grain prices reveal that there have been only two periods of five years when the price farmers received averaged as low a purchasing power, on the 1935-39 basis, as the $1.83 has had for the past five years. For the majority of all the 61 years the price received by farmers has given them a purchasing power for a bushel of wheat considerably higher than the purchasing power for the last five years at the price of $1.83.
That puts an entirely different light on the $1.83 a bushel, does it not? Then I go on to one more paragraph:
The initial price of $1.60, which farmers are now receiving under the international wheat agreement has, on a 1935-39 basis, a purchasing power of only 75 cents. This is the real reason why farmers today are so gravely discontented, for they find they simply cannot pay their high-cost 1951 bills with this depreciated Canadian currency and with the present price of wheat.
Now, I am quite sure that even the member who has interrupted me twice will realize that his points were very poorly taken when he reads this.
The member who interrupted wants to ask again whether you believe these Searle grain reports that you have read.
Let me ask the hon. member, who is so foolishly irresponsible he is making himself silly-
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. No member in this house can say that another member makes himself silly. I have yet to watch a sillier member than the hon. gentleman.
If the word "silly" is too strong-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish to say that the discussion should relate to the item under consideration.

I was just going to answer the hon. member who raised the question, and whose information concerning this matter seems to be utterly deficient for a man representing a western constituency, and I am asking if he questions the figures which are given by the dominion bureau of statistics publication, "Price Index Numbers of Commodities and Services used by Farmers, basis 1935-39". I do not think he will, but if he does it will make him look foolish, which is just as bad as silly.
Supply-Agriculture
Now, the next important matter is one which was developed by the member for Souris, and that is the comparative prices which farmers received in Canada as related to the prices which farmers in the United States received.
I am reading again from the Searle Grain Company report of March 28, 1951, on the last page. Once more I believe we shall find these figures are authentic. It reads as follows:
According to the United States government publication, Agricultural Prices, dated February 28, 1951, on page 8, the farmers of North Dakota received on February 15 at their country elevators for the average quality of wheat they hauled $2.24 a bushel compared with the price received by Canadian farmers at their average country points and for the average grade they delivered of $1.20. The Canadian average price is based on initial payment of $1.60 Fort William and for the average grades between No. 4 and No. 5. This prairie wheat, however, is being sold by the wheat board at $1.88 for No. 1 northern . .
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, my hon. friend says that he is giving authentic figures. Every member from western Canada at least knows that the farmers have not been selling wheat for $1.20.
I did not say $1.20.
It is down to 83 cents.

I shall read the details again since some of them might have confused the minister. I shall read the whole thing.
According to the United States government publication. Agricultural Prices, . . .
If these people are wrong, all right. I have always found these people to be correct, although I do not agree with them as to-
Then why call them to witness?
If you would just let me-
Order. Sit down.
An hon. member cannot call someone to witness if he is not going to rely on him.
The hon. member will cool down by tomorrow. The fact is, I do not agree with the Searle grain people as to-
Then do not call them to witness.

-their belief that we should sell our grain on the open market. I do not agree with them at all in that respect. However, I have never found their figures to be in error and I have been dealing with them for fifteen years.

Supply-Agriculture
I have been dealing with them for twenty years.

If the hon. member would just let a person speak and say what he has to say, the hon. member would' not make himself look foolish. The minister would like to hear this, so I shall read it again.
According to the United States government publication, Agricultural Prices, dated February 28, 1951, on page 8, the farmers of North Dakota received on February 15 at their country elevators for the average quality of wheat they hauled $2.24 a bushel compared with the price received by Canadian farmers at their average country points and for the average grade they delivered of $1.20.
Everyone knows that is not correct; that is the advance payment on wheat, it is not the price of the wheat delivered.
The minister is out of order.
It is only part of the price.
That is correct, but the advance payment is what the farmer has to live on.
That is not what the Searle report says, so what the Searle report says is not correct.

We will leave the minister to fight that out with them. This is based on the average grades, and when the minister examines the statement he will find he has not much to complain about.
The Canadian average price is based on initial payment of $1.60 Fort William and for the average grades between No. 4 and No. 5. This prairie wheat, however, is being sold by the wheat board at $1.88 for No. 1 northern, which might leave another 28 cents to come later as a final payment at the end of this crop year. Even so, however, Canadian farmers will still be receiving only $1.48 at country elevators, compared with the $2.24 being paid to North Dakota farmers.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to go any further into this matter tonight, but certainly at a future time I intend to go into it. As I said the other day in response to a speech by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent, those farmers who went into that great Palliser Triangle area some sixty years ago, and who have struggled against adverse conditions of numerous types for more than half a century, in season and out of season, those men who by sheer courage and selfsacrifice have made from that desert area, which Captain Palliser declared was unfit for farming, one of the most productive areas in Canada, are deserving of credit and aid. As witness of that fact let me cite the figure of over 1,425 million bushels of grain from western Canada sold during the time of the British-Canada wheat agreement-and that is the area that Captain Palliser said would not be fit for human habitation!

The point I am endeavouring to establish is this. If we are wise in Canada we will lend these people a helping hand so that they can roll out to us again the hundreds of millions of bushels of grain. All they are asking at this time is that they be returned some of the hundreds of millions of dollars which have been deliberately stolen from them by government policy. Anyone who laughs about that just emphasizes his own ignorance, because it is true, as the hon. member for Battle River and the hon. member for Acadia has shown. As I say, I am closing my remarks tonight, but this is not the last I am going to say in advocacy of the proposition that the dominion government at an early date contribute $48 million more to the pool fund for the farmers of western Canada.

When the minister makes his statement, I should like him to tell the house why he allowed the potato growers of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island to sell their potatoes below the cost of production. They were sold at practically half the cost of production. During the fall and most of the winter months, up till yesterday, they were sold below the cost of production in spite of the Agricultural Prices Support Act that was passed in this house in 1944. In 1947 the minister stated in this house that during the transition period he did not intend to allow any agricultural product to go below the cost of production, and he was not going to ask any farmer to cut down his production.
The potato business in the Saint John river valley and in New Brunswick has been built up over a period of 45 years. During the last war we sold potatoes under a ceiling. The farmers of that section sold their potatoes from $2 to $2.50 a barrel, when they could have sold them at $5 and $6 a barrel; but they kept within the ceiling price.
When the Agricultural Prices Support Act was put in force in 1944 we were promised that we would be protected on account of selling at ceiling prices during the period from peace to war, or as long as that act was in force. That act is still in force, and yet this fall potatoes were sold at as low as 20 cents a bushel. Most of the farmers who sold potatoes at that low price were veterans who took up land under the Veterans Land Act, or young farmers just starting in to farm. There was no protection for them. They were forced to sell their potatoes for as low as 20 cents a bushel, which is one-third of the cost of production or less. No action was taken by the government, although there was a committee of the marketing board and a committee of the

provincial government set up. We had delegations come to Ottawa and wait upon the Department of Agriculture no fewer than three times during that period. They never got any satisfaction or any relief whatever until they came here just before the Easter recess.
Then there was some plan worked out. No one knows yet what the plan is, only that the government has guaranteed on potatoes delivered to the starch factories a price of 22 cents a bushel, not over 22 cents a bushel. They do not guarantee that they will pay over that. They can pay under that. It will depend upon what the marketing boards of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick set as the price. If they set a price below 44 cents a bushel then the government will pay less than 22 cents a bushel, but the government through an arrangement with the provincial government, I believe, is going to pay the farmers if the marketing board price that the two provinces set is 44 cents a bushel. If it is that figure then they will pay 22 cents a bushel, or half of the 44 cents a bushel. Forty-four cents a bushel is the set price of the marketing board at the present time.
The farmer has to grade these potatoes, and they must be No. 1 potatoes. Twenty-five per cent of each load hauled to the starch factories can be No. 1 small. They do not get paid for the potatoes when they deliver them to the factory. The factory pays the 22 cents a bushel that they agreed to pay during the month of April, but the government gives them a participation certificate. I have heard a lot of talk in this house from the western members about participation certificates, but I never thought we would come to them in eastern Canada. I have heard discussions in this house about income tax. Our potato growers are not worrying this year about the income tax. They are *worrying about the sheriff coming in and putting them out of doors and forcing them into bankruptcy.
Potato growers in New Brunswick want whatever the government is going to give them, or the provincial government, or whatever government it is going to be. Whatever plan was made between the two governments they want it now because the banks are forcing them-

May I ask a question? Are
not the two starch factories in New Brunswick going to pay the farmers 60 cents a barrel? As I understand, that works out to 22 cents a bushel.

Yes.
Supply-Agriculture

Why is my hon. friend
giving the impression that the government is going to pay it? Why is he giving the impression that they are not going to be paid when the potatoes are delivered?

The starch factories pay
their 22 cents a bushel when the potatoes are delivered, but the government's 22 cents a bushel, which they have agreed to pay, is not going to be paid. They receive only a certificate for their 22 cents a bushel until the end of the season. It may be paid before the provincial election in Prince Edward Island. I do not know. That is all they are getting today. The government part of the bargain is a 22-cent participation certificate, being 22 cents a bushel. That certificate is no earthly good to the farmer. The farmers cannot take them to the bank and pay their notes for last year's fertilizer, and they are being forced into bankruptcy every day in our province and in the potato district.
This potato industry was built up as a $20 million industry in the province of New Brunswick. It has been built up over a period of years. The government has done very little toward the building up of that industry. The farmers and the shippers have spent their own money building up that industry, and now it is gone. They have sold their potatoes not only this year but for three years now at less than the cost of production. According to the act and according to the letters I received from Dr. Shaw last spring that was not supposed to happen. He said that the Agricultural Prices Support Act was supposed to help the farmers. This is what he said:
I would like to point out that the Agricultural Prices Support Act states:	"That the board shall
endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture . . . and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns for agriculture and those from other occupations."
